utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber will give its ruling on certain pending matters. With respect to the accused's 56th motion for finding of disclosure violations and for sanctions, Witness KDZ-029, which was filed yesterday, 18th of August, 2011, the Chamber has considered the arguments of the accused and the Prosecution's written response and finds that the Prosecution violated its obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) by failing to disclose the proofing note of KDZ-029 before the 7 May 2009 dead-line. However, the accused himself acknowledges that the "substance of the proofing note is not earth-shattering" and does not suggest that he has been prejudiced by this late disclosure. Having reviewed the one-page proofing note and considering the submissions of the parties, the Chamber finds that the accused will have sufficient time to consider this newly disclosed document and incorporate it if necessary in his cross-examination of KDZ-029. Given the length and content of the new material, the Chamber is not convinced that the accused has been prejudiced by this late disclosure. In these circumstances, the requested exclusion of KDZ-029's testimony is denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have filed a motion for subpoena for Christoph von Bezold, and in an attempt to make contact with him, we're told by the German authorities that they would not provide us with his contact details but that any correspondence should go through him -- through them and they would forward it to him. So on the 23rd of June we wrote a letter to Mr. von Bezold and sent it to the legal advisor here in The Hague for the German embassy, and we've heard nothing since then. Earlier this week I sent them another correspondence asking them if they could give us a report on whether they had been able to transmit that to Mr. von Bezold and whether they've had any response from him. So I'm hoping to hear from the German authorities in the next few weeks and I'll advise the Chamber as soon as I do, and I think once we've heard, then that matter will be ready for a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Unless there are any matters to be dealt with we'll bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, just going back for a moment to the issue of our correspondence with states, I just wanted to advise the Chamber that the Registry has taken the position that they won't serve any of our correspondence on the states, so that's why we make them filings. And the Trial Chamber earlier -- the Pre-Trial Chamber had actually ruled that they would not compel the Registry to serve our correspondence on states. As a result, when we initially tried to request documents from states, and I went around on my bicycle to the embassies and handed the letters there, we got no responses, so they treated it as junk mail. So we find that whenever we correspond with the states through the Registry, we do get responses, and when we drop our letters off by ourselves, we don't. So if you don't mind, we would like to find a way to continue to use the services of the Registry so that our communication with the states can be more productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard that, we will look into the matter again. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's probably because you're going on a bicycle, Mr. Robinson. Maybe if you took a limousine, they might take it rather more serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe I'll apply to OLAD for the funds for the limousine for that next time. Also, Mr. President, yesterday we received a motion from the Prosecution for -- notifying us that they had applied for a subpoena for one of their witnesses, and I just wanted to advise the Chamber that we won't be filing a response to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had also kindly asked just to say one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I would like to say that the ambitions of the Prosecution are not that small in respect of this witness. His amalgamated statement contains 88 pages, and they go into evidence. So the greatest masters of law are asking this simple man all sorts of questions, and he gives answers and all of this goes beyond his role, his education, and his profile as such. To put it bluntly, if this amalgamated statement is going to be admitted into evidence, the Defence is asking for considerably more time. If that will not be the case, Rule 92 ter will be seriously compromised. You saw for yourselves that it's much better when we have viva voce testimony. It is much easier to see whether it is the witness who is formulating his own thoughts or the Prosecution. So I'm asking for more time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has carefully considered various factors, including the scope of anticipated testimony and his 92 ter statements and concluded two and a half hours is sufficient for your cross-examination. There's no need to revisit the issue unless -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm -- I think the Court has already made a ruling, so I don't want to spend much time on this, but I think it's worth noting that the amalgamated statement is comprised of examination in court. So the submission is certainly unfounded to the extent it suggests otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the witness being brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. We apologise for the delay this morning. If you weren't advised, it didn't have anything to do with you, but it related to procedural matters that weren't connected with your testimony, so -- but those are completed and now we can begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go into private session for the next series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably due to some time constraint yesterday you forgot to read out the summary of this witness, but that should not have any impact upon our hearing. Are there any objection to the associate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would object to 65 ter number 0060 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just give me a minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're objecting to just one, 00604, the statement of Svetislav Mitrovic, also known as Niski. In this particular circumstance -- first of all, besides it being the statement of a third person, which we believe is not admissible, if you look at the evidence at page 24 of the witness's amalgamated statement, the statement was only used in the Krajisnik case so that the witness could identify the name of Niski. And so under those circumstances we don't believe that it's indispensable to the understanding of the previous testimony, and for those reasons we would ask that the Court not admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that falls within the ambit of the previous discussion, Your Honour, so I accept Mr. Robinson's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And with the exception of that exhibit, i.e., 65 ter 604, and those that have already been admitted, all the associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and given numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness. You'll be asked by Mr. Radovan Karadzic for his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to take the advantage of your giving testimony in order to shed some light on the events that took place at the very beginning. You confirmed yesterday your earlier statements that on the 8th of April you took your family across the Drina to Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you the only one who did that, or were other cases of the same nature?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many people like that. There were even my neighbours who were Muslims whom I transferred across.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right, then, to say that a situation emerged in which both the Muslims and the Serbs wanted at least their families, if not themselves, have transferred across to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all afraid of what the future would bring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you heard this from Victim and Witness Section. Could you please put a pause before you start answering the question, because both of you, Mr. Karadzic and you, are speak the same language. The interpreters have difficulty if you do not -- if you do overlap. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I will take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to apologise. We do overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what happened, and when did this situation begin, the situation which prompted you and all other Serbs, many other Serbs, and even some Muslims, to believe that it was necessary to take your families out of Zvornik to the right-hand side bank of the Drina into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was mutual mistrust setting in in town. The Serbs didn't believe the Muslims and vice versa. A corporal was killed in Sapna some 15 days ago [as interpreted], I think, before the conflict broke out. Nearly no Serbs came to work at the police station in fear of their lives. For that reason, the Serbian police station was set up in Karakaj and the Muslim remained behind. The Muslims were arming their fellow citizens instead of giving any weapons to the Serbs. So before any hostilities broke out and before we heard about this killing, there were already Muslims under arms a couple of days before the conflict. In Bijeljina they were already in street fully armed, and at that time they were already patrolling the streets. I was also patrolling the streets, but I was not armed. So they were controlling Zvornik until the night of 8th of April, five or six days before the conflict, and after that, the Serbs took over the control of Zvornik in spite of the fact that some Muslims remained in Zvornik. Since a soldier was killed in Zvornik near the department store, and he was fired at from Kula, I suppose, an action was launched to seize Kula because it dominates over Zvornik and there's forest there. So that was a very convenient place for them to hide. This is how I understood the situation in Zvornik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to simplify things a little. You were saying that there were many Muslims on the streets under arms. Were those long-barrelled arms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even saw a submachine-gun carried by one man. That was the first time I saw such a weapon. Although I was working in the technical department, I had never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were those regular police forces that one could have trusted, or were those some different citizens? Were some people among them who were unreliable or even criminals? And I'm talking about people patrolling the street.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go downtown at the time, but I did hear that there were criminals with long-barrelled firearms. As for the rest, they were all members of the Zvornik TO. An appeal was broadcast on the Radio Zvornik inviting the citizens to defend the town. However, the radio station was controlled by the Muslim officials. And my neighbours were already in my neighbourhood, or people from thereabout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, how come that ordinary people and even criminals had so many weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably in compliance with our All People's Defence system there was -- there were arms in depots for the army and the reserve police, and they probably -- these weapons intended for reserve police were distributed to Muslims. And the TO warehouse, which belonged to the army and was intended for defence, was situated in Zvornik. And before the conflict, that was where the Zvornik TO depot was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned that the Muslims took all the weapons from the depot that belonged to the police, that the Serbian policemen relocated to Karakaj, to the Serbian part of Zvornik. Does that mean that the Muslims had MUP weapons in their hands and only later the Serbs managed to take control of the TO depot?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, one might say that. It was possible for people to obtain weapons in Mali Zvornik. Those were our weapons from Zvornik, as well as the uniforms, ammunition, and everything else. Well, how this was transferred over there I don't know, because I reported only on the 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm sure the witness is -- is trying to comply with the Court's encouragement to pause, but it's, of course, difficult to know. I noted that the Court sometimes suggest to witnesses to watch the cursor and see when that ends and that's -- that's a helpful way of knowing when the translation has been completed. You may want to mention that to the witness as a technique for identifying when the translation has concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take that into account, sir. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from the weapons that belonged to the MUP or the reserve police, were there any other weapons? Did the parties involved procure weapons? Did the Muslims receive weapons from some quarters and did the Serbs later also receive weapons, or was it taken from these regular depots that under the law were controlled by the municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is most probably the case, but I cannot confirm how either of the side procured their weapons. Probably they did it in the way you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one say that in the Muslim part of Zvornik, excluding Karakaj, from the 4th or the 5th of April until the 9th of April, only a handful of Serbs remained and that nearly all of them had left either to Karakaj or to Serbia? Can you please wait with your answer.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Many Serbs left Zvornik, particularly those who were living in apartment blocks. Only a few of them remained. Even in my neighbourhood there were many Serb families, and in this period after the 9th of April, only five or six of us remained there on the street where I lived. People who lived in the centre of town in apartment blocks, once they saw who was patrolling the town, they immediately left. On the afternoon of the 8th of April, a bus was put to block the bridge which prevented anyone leaving Zvornik by car. When I wanted to return to Zvornik, I had to go through Karakaj and then through the Scemlija village. I had to take this village road in order to reach my house where my mother and father and brother were, and I wanted to take them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who blocked the bridge by putting the bus there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Muslims. At Vidakova Njiva, which is the exit point towards Karakaj, they also erected a roadblock on the 6th or 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me -- but just one more question. Did anyone persuade the Serbs to leave, or did they reach their own conclusions and were they afraid when they saw who was patrolling the streets under arms?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid for the security of my family. That's why I took them away. But I myself returned to Zvornik. Generally speaking, everybody was afraid of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sometimes you say you returned on the 13th, and in another testimony of yours, on the first page of -- second page of your amalgamated statement you say that you returned on the same day, the 8th. It is not exactly important, but can you tell us if you returned on the 8th and reported for mobilisation, or did you return on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned on the 8th of April. During the fight for Zvornik, I was in my home. I went to Scemlija. My mother, myself, my two Serbian neighbours, and two Muslim neighbours went there. I remained there until the afternoon. My mother and my brother and the Muslims left earlier. I remained in Scemlija. I exited the town via Tomanici Escilja [phoen]. After that I went back to Serbia once again on the 9th of April, and then I came back on the 13th and reported at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slow down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In addition to putting a pause between question and answer, could you kindly slow down as well when you speak. Very kind, thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have clarified this. It is correct that you returned on the same day and that you returned on the 13th. Do you remember that on the 4th of April the Rump Presidency of BH made up of Muslim and Croat members declared general mobilisation, and apart from the killing of the JNA column and mobilisation itself, contributed to the emergence of such a huge number of unauthorised people bearing long-barrelled arms and weapons on the streets of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that contributed to this, even the killing of the wedding party in Sarajevo. This undermined the trust of citizens, not only in Zvornik but in other places as well, because at that time we were all watching the news and trying to get as much information as possible. We don't know how correct and accurate they were, but we were all very much involved regardless of our ethnicity in following what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice then that a slaughter took place in Sijekovac on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that covered by the media?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, possibly, but I myself cannot confirm that. I'm not 100 per cent sure that I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were aware that there was a crisis in Bijeljina. Did that have an impact on the fear instilled in the Serbs in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, that was not the only factor that caused fear among the Serbs. They went out in Bijeljina walking around the town bearing weapons, and that was a very strong psychological effect. We were just concerned about the possibility of trying to avoid any conflict. Although we Serbs had some weapons, we decided not even to display any handguns in order to avoid being blamed for the conflict, because when you have two sides who are armed, there will always be somebody who is foolish enough to pull out his weapon and fire, because the atmosphere was such. There was something in the air indicating that a conflict was going to erupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you reported to the Crisis Staff in response to mobilisation. Was that also in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence, that is to say, that it was the municipality that was in charge of defence, and in some of your statements you said just like the president of the state is the Commander-in-Chief, likewise the president of municipality is the Commander-in-Chief with respect to the defence of a municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an All People's Defence system before the war, so all members of a certain age, after they finished their compulsory military service were members of the TO or the reserve police. So that applied to the civilians who were also mobilised. I automatically was a member of the TO, and subsequently I became a member of the armed forces. Of course, one had to know who was in charge. All these operations were administered and run by the president of the municipality, although we had staff commanders, but he was in charge of the civilian side of that. I presume that they were constantly discussing and agreeing how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik issued this call, and that is what you said in pages 2 and 3 of your amalgamated statement. You said that everybody, regardless of their ethnicity, was called up, and you said that at that time, Serbs remained living in the Serbian part of Zvornik, as well as some Muslims, that they responded as well, and that you set up joint patrols; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all there, the Serbs and the Muslims alike. Zuca told me, "Let Serbs patrol also, and this will improve our chances of maintaining the law and order."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He said something -- actually, Stevo Radic said something similar. He said, "It is not important if a person is a Muslim. He is a citizen of the town, and let him patrol, because that's his place of residence."

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have many contacts with Stevo Radic in that period. I just applied for a pass for going to Serbia and for movement around town. Most frequently, because Stevo Radic was busy, I contacted Zuco, but Stevo Radic did tell me that he agrees for both the Muslims and the Serbs to patrol together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at what you say at the top of page 5 of your amalgamated statement, which corroborates what you just said. This has been attributed to Radic, but you say that Zuca maintained a similar position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then there's a reference here to a Muslim on page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I kindly ask Mr. Tieger for his assistance. Do we need to go into private session since it has to do with a personal relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think Dr. Karadzic thoughtfully raises a good point, but the answer is no. Two things: As I indicated to Mr. Robinson yesterday, we attempted to indicate as clearly as possible whether a matter previously was addressed in open or private session, and one can see that under the page references. So that's a helpful way of indicating that. I appreciate that there may be circumstances which give rise to confidentiality concerns otherwise, but I don't think this is one. I think it was raised in that manner before. And by way of clarification about something the accused said earlier, I think that the reference at the top of page 5 was not attributed to Radic but was attributed in -- if one looks at the beginning of that passage at the bottom of page 4 and continuing on to page 5, it's clearly a reference consistent with what the witness said in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I also prefer to remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did have an opportunity of seeing that the late Sejfudin Hadziefendic was brought in, and in passing you were asked whether you knew him, and you said when you identified him in the car, you said that you knew him and that he was a good man and that he should be released and that they should apologise to him; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Sejfudin is not Hadziefendic, he is Hadziavdic. I said that because I had knowledge from 1991, as far as back as that, and we knew each other for many years before that. When there was this conflict this Croatia, because we all knew that humanitarian aid was being sent to Croatia, it wasn't being sent to Serbs, it was sent to Croats in Croatia, he asked me then how he could provide humanitarian aid to the Krajina, and I said through the Red Cross from Serbia. And he did what I said. He said, "(redacted) that is what I did." And knowing all of that, that he is a hard working and honest man, when I saw who it was, that is why I said what I said, that he's an honest and that he is a fair man. I did not say that he sent aid to Serbs in Croatia I just said that he was an exceptionally fair and honest man and that they should release him and that nobody should touch him and that they should apologise to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these were very dramatic times, right? You were not some office-holder in the government. Basically you were an ordinary citizen. They asked you about that man. Is it correct that they released him and that they apologised to him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they released him and apologised to him. After these clashes, when he came to see me he told me about that. We did not discuss it at length. He just said, "It's all right that they listened to what you said. They took me back, and they apologised for having done what they did."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I had the amount of time that I had asked for, every answer of yours would have been precious to me, no matter how extensive. However, in view of how short our time is, let us try to keep your answers as short as possible whenever possible. Does that mean that the persons who brought him in cared about whether he actually did something or not and whether he was an honest man?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are two questions there, whether he had done something and whether he was an honest man. My answer yes, he's an honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And those who detained him, was that important for them to realise whether he was an honest man or whether he had done something wrong?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7 now of your amalgamated statement -- actually, I'd like us to make a distinction. Do you agree that in our system, before the Army of Republika Srpska was established, there was a municipal brigade of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a municipal brigade of the Territorial Defence. There was a detachment of the TO. As for the establishment of this brigade and the municipality and the Army of Republika Srpska, that is when the brigade was formed and then the detachment no longer existed. The detachment could also have several battalions like the brigade did, so it's similar but the formulation is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the Army of Republika Srpska came into being on the 20th of May, after the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So up until the 20th of May, there was a detachment of the Territorial Defence that was under civilian control of the Crisis Staff and under the command of the commander of the TO of the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the staff of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After having reported from the 13th of April until the 3rd or 4th of May, you were given a task by the Crisis Staff to patrol the streets, and you did that with one or two Muslims who had also been given that assignment by the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 4th of May, you were told that you should report to the commander of the Territorial Defence, and you waited for them all day because they were somewhere at the front line facing Sapna and Nezuk. Were they attacking Sapna and Nezuk, or were the Muslims from Sapna and Nezuk attacking the Serb part of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether they were attacking, but they were in Sapna and Nezuk. In the evening, sometime on the 4th or 5th, Aco Sekanic saw me, and I then reported on the morning of the 6th to the Crisis Staff, to the TO staff, in order to get a particular assignment. So that was St. George's Day. And they went to Nezuk. Now, why? For which reason? I really cannot say because I was not in contact with them, so I had no way of knowing. About these details, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who had Sapna and Nezuk under their control? You say "they." Were Sapna and Nezuk in Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sapna and Nezuk were under Muslim control, like Zaselak [phoen] and a few other villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 8, we see what kind of work you were assigned, and that was in line with your VES, that is to say, your military speciality that you were assigned while serving in the JNA, while doing your military service, compulsory military service; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the Army of Republika Srpska was established on the 20th of May, and then sometime in the beginning of June, the Zvornik Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For a short period of time the commander of that brigade was Mr. Blagojevic; right? And then -- and then he was replaced -- actually, can you help us with that? Who replaced Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Vasilic, Bobe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Thank you. That has nothing to do with the Vasilic who was in the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Vasilic not Vasovic. But, all right, that can be corrected in the transcript. Now I'd like us to specify something. The municipality kept the infrastructure of the Territorial Defence, which is owned by the municipality anyway; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was still a commander of the Territorial Defence, and there was -- there were still depots of the Territorial Defence, and in a way they were supposed to be under the supervision of the army, but basically they are a municipal institution; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The depot of the Territorial Defence that was in Mali Zvornik was not functioning until the 19th of May because all the materiel and technical resources that were there were transferred to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To familiarise the Trial Chamber with this, while there was still a single state, Mali Zvornik was on the right bank of the river and is in Serbia, and Zvornik, which is on the other side of the river in Bosnia, it was one and the same thing while there was a single state; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was only the Drina River that was between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean the Serb municipality of Zvornik because it remained without any infrastructure of the MUP and without the weapons of the MUP and without the weapons of the Territorial Defence of companies and enterprises that are in the urban area, does that mean that they took over their municipal property from Mali Zvornik and transferred it to the Bosnian part of Zvornik, to Zvornik as such, and that they established a depot there and the infrastructure of the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That seems an enormously complicated question that also builds in some facts not in evidence, so I think it needs to be deconstructed and commenced again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you break down the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that we had established that, that the entire infrastructure and the weaponry of the MUP had remained in Muslim hands; whereas the infrastructure of the Territorial Defence remained in Mali Zvornik and that the Serbs took it over and returned it to the Serb municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And I would also emphasise that that relates to particular periods of time. I understand that Mr. Dr. Karadzic is now in May. I think the previous answer referred to sometime in early April, and I think in order to have any clarity at all, those matters need to be raised discretely and clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a word, the Serb municipality of Zvornik, did it transfer the weaponry and depot of the Territorial Defence across the river and establish their own depot?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's April. And then up until the 19th of May, it was only natural that people went to their own warehouse and that's in Serbia, but then that turned out to be a different state. At the time I was involved in the transportation of this equipment from Serbia to our depots that were in Standard and even in the atomic shelter of the Birac factory, because we had three hangars there where our equipment was, and we could not find enough room for all of that in Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that in the Serb part of Zvornik, or, rather, the Serb municipality of Zvornik, Karakaj, Alhos, Standard, and Glinica, all of them are there in this area that was always populated by Serbs. Had there not been a war, it would have been the Serb municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the population there was 99.99 per cent Serb. But the Glinica Alumina factory had their own weapons and other weapons had their own weapons, but all of that was within the system of All People's Defence in the depots in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 11 of your amalgamated statement you say that some people, that is to say, this Pavlovic, he actually had a different name and you found out about that much later. Can one say that sometimes people did falsely represent themselves either in terms of their name or the office they held or the importance they had? Were there situations where people would come and introduce themselves in a certain way but that way would turn out to be false or exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I did not really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it only this Pavlovic who used a false name when introducing himself, or were there other people who introduced themselves by using certain nicknames or were they using their own names but inventing offices and positions they held?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavlovic falsely represented himself at the time, because later I found out that his name was Branislav Popovic. Other persons just introduced themselves by their nicknames. They did not give their first and last names. So quite a few people were known by their nicknames. As for the particular offices that they held -- how do I put this? It was either in the municipality or in the brigade. They decided who would hold which position and where. As far as I can understand your question, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we'll have break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the republican organs had not declared a state of war ever on the level of the whole republic and only seldom they did it partially?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that it wasn't declared. The only thing that was declared was an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that under such conditions civilian structures exist, including the Territorial Defence, and that it was the civilian authorities who were in charge of the territory and the army was in charge of the front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long the process of constituting and equipping the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade last? Was it up until sometime in mid-June?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forming of the brigade started towards the end of May, and they gave their solemn oath on the St. Vitus Day, on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just now establish a clear distinction between the situation that prevailed until the 28th of June and the one after that. Is it true that volunteers reported to the municipal authorities, whether you wish to call them a Crisis Staff, the Presidency of the municipality or interim government? Did they report it in keeping with the law and the decision of the SFRY Presidency stipulating that volunteers were a legitimate and regular force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question relating to the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, was it regulated by law and was it legal for volunteers to report?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were local people subject to military obligation, whereas those who were not subject to that obligation, that they came from other countries such as Serbia, Montenegro, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We who were locals had an obligation to defend ourselves and to be part of those units. As for them, I don't know exactly to whom they reported once they arrived. However, later on they were all assigned to the brigade units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us establish that they came, they were assigned to TO brigades, and when they formed their separate units, such as Pivarski, Niski, Yellow Wasps, et cetera, it turned out that there were many local conscripts in those units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of battalion. More than 80 per cent of local residents were in Zuco's voluntary units, in Zuco's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one say, and that can be inferred from many statement of yours, that the majority of the volunteers, both those who came from elsewhere and the local ones, that they were all patriots, that they were good people and well behaved on the line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of them were well behaved. However, there were isolated incidents and misbehaviour. Nobody can deny that, but that was happening everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 13 of your statement. You were asked in open session in another case about who issued tasks, and it was established that after St. Vitus Day, the 28th of June, when the brigade became official and legitimate, it was possible for Marko Pavlovic as well to give orders to the Territorial Defence, whereas the commander of the brigade issued orders to his troops.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know what kind of co-operation existed between Marko Pavlovic and the brigade commander. I don't know what kind of meetings they had, but it is true that both of them issued assignments and gave assignments to the conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were a reserve officer. Did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a non-commissioned officer, more specifically a corporal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now on page 13. Tell me, does this look to you as some kind of state of dual authority, because both were entitled to issue orders?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can say that because within the defence system, if you have a regular unit, such as brigade, it's up to them to issue. However, what they're going to agree mutually between themselves, what was important for the responsibility of the brigade, I cannot go into those details. The situation was such that the military conscripts should receive orders only by the brigade commander regarding their activities. That is what I think, at least, because by the very fact of the brigade being formed, all of us who had been before that in Territorial Defence Staff were transferred to this unit, both the reserve officers and active-duty officers, and we were supposed to receive orders directly from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that didn't happen immediately; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the establishment of detachment, this was still not a practice. This happened maybe after I left detention. While I was in detention that was the situation, but after that Marko Pavlovic actually left Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have confirmed that Marko Pavlovic, and that's on page 13, that Marko Pavlovic had some kind of certificate testifying that he was a member of the VRS. Did he need such a certificate in order to pass through the army check-points, because army did not recognise this dual status?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This certificate was issued to him when he left Zvornik on the 28th of August in order for him to be able to regulate his status outside the territory of Republika Srpska. That's what I think, because before that, he himself could have signed such a certificate, and he was authorised to issue documents of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the fact that everyone who appeared on the lines would receive orders from the regional commander of the brigade in its area of responsibility. It is true that although there was no war, whoever appeared on the line, be it the police, the volunteers, the Territorial Defence, had to be resubordinated to the local brigade commander in his area of responsibility. Was that a customary practice?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be. But it wasn't the case on many occasion, because the civilian authorities had their command, and the police, for example, ignored the orders coming from the brigade commander because they had a different structure. Perhaps the reason for that was that only an imminent state of war was declared rather than a state of war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from your answer on page 16, where you say that you were not quite sure who was issuing assignments, do you agree that after the brigade was formed, that is to say, from early July onwards, there was a certain confusion in terms of the authority and who was commanding whom and who was under whom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that many people were confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 17 you speak about the manner in which equipment and materiel were issued from the Territorial Defence depot. What was required was for someone to write a requisition order or something like that. Somebody has to approve it, and then the required equipment is issued in compliance with what was approved, not what was requisitioned. Now, this whole procedure, was that something that was inherited from the previous system, or was it something new?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was something inherited from the previous system, because the practice was, first of all, to have an order about operations, and after that, ammunition would be requisitioned from the depot, but it was issued according to the approval. It was well known how many kits were required for how many soldiers. If somebody asked for 10.000 rounds of ammunition, they couldn't receive only 5, because what had to be taken into account was the imminent operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If those who were deployed on the front line were responsible and answerable to the brigade commander, who were all these groups accountable during the periods when they were not on the front line but in town?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you to whom they were accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 17 you mention Pivarski. Did Pivarski hail from that area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pivarski is from Croatia. He was born somewhere in the vicinity of Vukovar or Borovo Selo. I don't know exactly. All I know is that he was from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the majority of his fighters also from that local area or did they come from some place else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of volunteers came from outside, but I don't know where from. However, 70 to 80 per cent of all these units, Niski, Pivarski, Zuco, accounted or were made up of our local fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that up until the 1st of July, the Territorial Defence and then the brigade, after the 1st of July, could have raised objections to the fact that local people were members of the formations that were being treated as volunteer units and later on as paramilitary? Was there any criticism with respect to local people being there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no objections, because we from the command assigned people to that unit. Whether that was done by the TO staff or the brigade, that was how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the time of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also about the time when the brigade was formed. So military conscripts, local conscripts, were assigned to those very units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that these units got some names, and most often they liked to call themselves special units. Was there an authorised organ that gave them that name, special units, or did they call themselves that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who gave them these attributes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you haven't seen a single document on the basis of which a unit was proclaimed a special unit or something like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen anything like that. Because, actually, I didn't have any documents that were accessible to me in view of the position that I held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a reserve junior officer or non-commissioned officer or junior sergeant, as you had put it, in peacetime after you did your military service, were you called up for military exercises?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One month after demobilisation I was called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you employed somewhere at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many times did you spend on these drills or military exercises?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, seven or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During those seven or ten days, were you provided with a salary by your company or by the military department, or did the military department reimburse your company?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996, when I attended this military exercise, nobody refunded my salary, because beforehand it was the Ministry of Defence that carried out these obligations until 1991 in the case of such military exercises. Afterwards, no one could afford that, but I did file an application, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I was actually referring to the period before this war. Once you did your military service, your compulsory military service, you were given this rank and then you were called up for military exercises; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in that period I was given a salary in view of the rank that I held and also my salary was reimbursed and I was given per diems. That was before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. That was the system. Either the company would pay out your salary and it would be reimbursed by the ministry, or the ministry would pay it directly to you if you were not employed; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The municipal Territorial Defence, the system of Territorial Defence, did it inherit the very same system? Namely, if persons are not employed, then they pay them directly, whereas if they are employed, they are paid by their salary. So this is not taken out of their own salaries.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was during the war too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us not try to find the documents now. Did you know that there were payrolls for persons who were not employed anywhere and who were engaged by the Territorial Defence and then the municipality paid them; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that how you received your salary?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until when and from whom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The payroll was provided to the brigade. I was in the brigade at the time. While I was in the brigade, that is when I received a salary. And I received a salary for the month of June, because that's when I was placed on this list, and I received a salary for the month of June. In the beginning of July, I was transferred to Zuco's unit, and I did not receive a salary for the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that after that first place that you were dismissed from, you received a salary for that from the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, if necessary, can we just briefly move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So volunteers from the Territorial Defence were receiving salaries from the municipality -- or, rather, the Territorial Defence, although 70 or 80 per cent of them were locals; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned several times, and you confirmed here that most of these volunteers were fair, proper, good fighters, patriots. Is that a reason why many arrested persons were released very soon after their arrest?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that many volunteers were fair and honest. I said that a large number of the fighters who were in the units. That did not only refer to volunteers but it referred to locals as well. I said that they were fair, that they were honest, and that in all units and among people in general, there are all kinds. As for this second question, why some people were released earlier and we were released later, in my opinion and in the opinion of most of us who remained in detention, and that's most probably the case anyway, we were kept because of Pale and because of the check-point. That is the reason why we were kept there, because all the others were released after seven or eight days, many volunteers, many locals as well. It's not only that volunteers were kept. Seven or eight of us were kept in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the rest? They were deployed to other units, and these existing units ceased to exist actually; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other volunteers from the groups of Niski and Pivarski were deployed in other units; whereas volunteers from Zuco's group, that is to say, persons who were not from that area, they were transferred to Mitrovica. They did not stay in our region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a list was compiled of 41 or 43 persons who were banned from Republika Srpska after that? Did that relate to those individuals, those who were transferred to Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about this list. That was not accessible to me anyway. However, afterwards, as for one of these persons who was detained with me, I saw him in Republika Srpska again. He was not in our region. I saw him at a different front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 22, I'd like to deal with the question of what you were suspected of. Was it assistance, contacts, collaboration with the Muslims? Am I correct that in terms of contact with Muslims and helping Muslims, no one would have held it against you, but they would hold it against you if it were collaboration, because that would have meant contact with the Muslim armed forces; right? That's not what you did; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not that. We did not do that. We did help whenever we could save someone. There were foolish people who didn't do that. There were people like that among us, like anywhere else, but we proceeded from the following: Do not do unto others what you would not want done to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that some crimes were committed anyway -- I actually had to find the reference here, but you can confirm it anyway. Is it correct that some persons committed crimes in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we're in open session now, because I'd have to mention something. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We'll go back -- we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could have a page reference quickly, please. I know approximately where it is, but it would be helpful to locate it immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little patience. I'll do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've got it now. And the reason I asked for it is I thought that was in private session previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 36. And I think we therefore need to be in private session again, and therefore we need a redaction for the previous portions of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Since that was the answer I gave, I'm afraid that it might happen that my name be mentioned and that somebody would establish the connection, because I would have to say what I was doing specifically, and that would be probably sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can put general questions, and after that we can move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there were check-points established. Can you tell us whether that was the case from April until mid-July? What kind of check-points were established, and what was controlled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one at Crni Vrh, which was manned by the military police and army in general in order to secure safe passage of the vehicles going to Sekovici and Pale or to Serbia, and there was another check-point in Zvornik, in Karakaj. But there were also points in Bijeljina, because they also checked whether conscripts were passing through, avoiding to join their units. So everything was under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the army was controlling what was in their domain, that is to say, the transportation of equipment, ammunition, materiel, and the passage of deserters; is that correct? Whereas the civilian police was in charge of controlling the regularity of cargo, vehicles, supporting documents and things of that nature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion and as far as I know what the situation on the ground was, everybody was controlling everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you know that under the law, the police was not authorised to control the army and that army was not authorised to control civilian affairs, and there was a conflict between Mr. Tolimir and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the name of the officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreter couldn't hear after "Mr. Tolimir and."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Davidovic, as a member of the civilian authorities, the police, stopped a major, frisked him, perhaps he even detained him, and General Tolimir -- actually, we showed this document when Mr. Davidovic testified here. General Tolimir protested, and that is something that was not allowed. Is that regulated by law, the military is not allowed to conduct civilian police work, and the civilian police is not allowed to do military police work?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be as a rule, but that's not the way it was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the cases when this did not happen on the ground these were violations of the law; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general could write up a report saying that this man had violated the law. However, when a civilian policeman brings me in as a military conscript, is that a violation of the law or not? But that did happen, indeed, with military conscripts in the town of Zvornik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the check-point near the front line at Crni Vrh, the military part was controlled by the military, and the police part -- actually, was there a police part of the check-point at Crni Vrh? Was there a police team there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a police team there. There was only a military team there, because policemen were standing only at the crossing on the bridge between the two states, Republika Srpska and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in Zvornik, the army was not exercising this control but it was the police, and at Crni Vrh, it wasn't the police but the army; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that at Crni Vrh it wasn't the police that was exercising control. There was no control whatsoever exercised by the police in Zvornik as regards the check-point. It was only at the crossing at the bridge that they looked at documents. They were not exercising any other control. Only sometimes they would arrest military conscripts who were in town, and as a rule, military men should be arrested by the military police not the civilian police, but this kind of thing did happen. The civilian police sometimes arrested military men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we actually have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me also -- can you please tell me how much time I'm going to be given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour, after which you'll have 35 minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'm afraid we have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I am mistaken here, but maybe not. Anyway, was the car returned to you? The other items were given back to you, but the car that was found in that yard, was that returned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the car that was found in the yard was not returned to me, and it wasn't even my car. As for my own car, it was returned, and they had difficulty locating where the car actually was, because it was not on the premises of Bijeljina MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on to the arrest itself, and let's deal with that topic. Now, do you recall that before the arrest in Zvornik, the unit of Mico Davidovic's, which had come as -- for -- as support, as a support unit, after my address to Panic and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but I'm fairly certain that the arrest is also a matter covered in private session. I don't think the preliminary matters Mr. Karadzic has addressed have created any problem, but if he's moving on to the arrest itself, that's where we'll be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your warning. Yes. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Well, as 170 persons were arrested, I thought this could not really help anyone identify any of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. What matters is whether it was in private session in the previous proceedings. That's the practice we are taking at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, of course, ultimately the issue is going to involve this witness, and he'll be moving toward his own involvement, and it will narrow that field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we go into private session? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, that will be admitted as Exhibit D1638. Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for five minutes for myself. If you can go on without me, then that would be fine. Otherwise, let us take a five-minute break so that I could refresh myself, because I'm quite exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Either way is -- well, not either way is fine -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's more prudent to take a break for five minutes. We'll break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 1.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I will also endeavour to be as efficient as possible with the very few questions and documents I'd like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But for your information, Ms. Elliott, I wonder if there's a point of continuing with the next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- given the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think we're probably at that point, Your Honour, and we were having the same discussion here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I need to move into private session for this first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd next like to ask you about a matter that was raised earlier today and that referred back to something that you said yesterday as well. That was at page 18 today. And there were several questions in connection with this, I believe, but Mr. Karadzic asked you about access to MUP weapons, which ethnic group had weapons and was displaying weapons and so forth. For example, at page 18, yesterday -- the question was: "Yesterday, you mentioned that the Muslims took all the weapons from the depot that belonged to the police," and asked whether that meant that the Muslims had MUP weapons in their hands and only later the Serbs managed to take control of the TO depot. I'd like to quickly show you 65 ter 00654. And I would ask to direct the witness's attention -- it might be helpful to show the next page first, just indicate what that is for the witness, in both English and B/C/S, and then again the next page after that. So this is a MUP document from Zvornik, Mr. Witness, outlining some work activities and some retrospective information from 1992 as well. And if we could turn to page 20 in e-court of the English and page 17 of the B/C/S. And if I could ask you to look at the middle of the page in B/C/S. And it should be, I believe, toward the bottom of the page in English where the report indicates that working on various check-points during the months of January and February. Again, this is - if we could look toward the top of the page - referring back to 1992. Police personnel of Serb nationality enabled the transport of weapons, ammunition, and other materiel and technical equipment necessary for the arming of the Serb people in the territory of this municipality. First, Mr. Witness, let me just ask you, very specifically, whether you were aware of activity by Serbian members of the MUP to ensure that members of the Serb community were armed prior to the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-340 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say in relation to the operation of the Zvornik public security station in that period is that it was not the Serbian policemen who took weapons from the MUP in Zvornik, but it was the Muslims who controlled the situation. There were more of them at the station, and they were in charge of the whole management. As far as I know, the arming in that period was assisted by the policemen but in such a way that they were able to load it from Mali Zvornik and transfer it to the other side. However, what they exactly did in that respect, I don't know. As for the weapons that remained in MUP, the Muslims took and distributed amongst themselves. The Serbian policemen were checking the bridges and everything, which enabled the transfer from the depot in Mali Zvornik to Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He didn't confirm anything, and then he just put specific part of almost 60-page document. What is the point of admitting this through this witness, Mr. Tieger? But I note the time. I'm very much concerned about time. You will have another opportunity to tender this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think -- first of all, I think there was confirmation the arming in that period was assisted by the policemen. Second, there's no dispute about the authenticity and relevance of this document. I have been extremely liberal with Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic in their use of documents in a similar manner. I didn't expect that a document that's clearly relevant to this issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have more questions, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't. That was my last question, Your Honour. I do tender this document again, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't -- there's two issues. This paragraph, whether that should be admitted, you can decide that, but a 60-page document shouldn't be admitted simply because one paragraph has been referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you happy with admitting this page and the cover page, probably?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't accept that as a general proposition. I think we haven't been doing that, but under the circumstances and in light of the time, I realise that's a way to move us forward at the moment and I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates your understanding. The two pages will be admitted as Exhibit P3183. Sir, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll rise altogether, and have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of August, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
